legacy_root.question: Extension ecosystems enforce declared permissions at runtime because the payload is code - when the payload is a prompt or a rule that merely PERSUADES an agent, what does a declared permission actually constrain, and is the honest answer that only the tool layer can enforce anything?
legacy_root.answer: A declared permission on a prompt, skill, or rule payload constrains nothing at the prompt layer. Chrome/WebExtensions can enforce a manifest permission because the payload is code and the browser calls PermissionsData::HasAPIPermission at the privileged-API boundary (ENFORCED). This program's skill/rule/plugin payloads are markdown that persuades an agent. Claude Code documents `allowed-tools` as a GRANT that 'does not restrict which tools are available'; permission rules and PreToolUse hooks (the tool layer) are what actually deny calls. Live fixtures here inject a Read-only skill/rule that requests Write: the prompt layer does not stop it; the same Write is blocked by the host allowlist and no file is written. Treating skill/rule declared permissions as a control is security theatre. Honest answer: only the tool layer can enforce anything.
legacy_root.honest_answer: only the tool layer can enforce anything
